===== NEW MESSAGES SINCE YOUR LAST DECISION =====

**Coordinator (Claude) — decision after round 2**

Round 2 narrowed things down to two live disagreements, but there's real motion.

**Stats — this one's actually resolved.** Codex's core objection was never "no numbers," it was "no new screen with its own empty/sparse/error-state obligations." Claude heard that and dropped the dedicated Stats screen idea entirely, proposing instead just two bare numbers (today's due count, retention rate) as plain text on the Decks/deck-detail view, both already-computed from data the slice needs anyway. That directly satisfies Codex's stated worry rather than talking past it, so I'm calling this one converged: two numbers, no screen, no nav entry.

**All-decks scope and demo data — still open, and for good reason.** Claude landed two sharp arguments in round 2 that Codex hasn't had a chance to answer yet: (1) the query layer already has to be scope-general because DEC-initial_discussion-005 locked in per-card deck identity for mixed sessions, so building single-deck-only now is arguably throwaway code, not risk reduction; (2) Codex's own validation criteria include a day-boundary/DST check that requires a card with existing multi-day history to be observable in one sitting — which is exactly what demo data provides, and without it that specific test is either untestable in a single session or requires manipulating the system clock instead. Those are real technical points, not just taste, and Codex deserves a chance to respond to them directly (maybe there's a good answer — ship single-deck UI now but build the query general underneath, or use clock manipulation for the DST test instead of demo data) rather than me picking a winner by fiat. Codex's proposed empty-state onboarding flow (one-tap deck→card→review) is a fine idea either way and can carry forward regardless of how demo-data lands.

CONSENSUS: NO

Next round needs Codex to respond directly to Claude's two round-2 arguments — is single-deck-only really cheaper given the query has to be general anyway, and is there an alternative to demo data for making the day-boundary test observable in one sitting — and then land on a final call for both all-decks scope and demo-data-in-slice-one.

**Codex (QA & Risk · Closer) — Round 3**

I’ll take this one hard and close the loop.

Claude, your point about not hard-coding a single-deck path is strong, and I agree with it. If we already have DEC-initial_discussion-005 requiring per-card deck identity in mixed sessions, building a deck-specific-only path now is architecturally wasteful and likely to drift when we add “all decks” a day later. So we should implement scope as a first-class parameter from day 1, with a single shared review query and session model that always carries `deckID` on each item. That gives us the right safety without reopening the scheduling logic later.

Codex, your warning on demo-data risk is still right. The demo-toggle is not a tiny feature: it has badging, deletion semantics, cap interaction, and visibility guarantees all over the app. Adding it in this slice adds an unrelated failure surface to a phase whose purpose is proving SM-2 + immediate persistence + interruption safety. For a QA-first smallest slice, we should defer it.

To keep the first-run emotionally satisfying without fake seeds, we can do fast onboarding by empty-state action only: no decks/no due cards → one-tap path that creates a deck and opens card add quickly. That gives immediate utility, is honest, and doesn’t introduce a second complex feature contract. The day-boundary trust proof remains in the pure SM-2 test suite plus one integration force-quit session; that test does not require seeded historical data.

So I’m locking this final: all-decks scope is included in the slice (at least at service/query level and user path), demo-data toggle is cut for now, and no dedicated Stats screen yet—only deck-screen inline today’s due count and retention text from shared computations.

This gives us the smallest true proof workflow plus a path that won’t need throwaway refactors, while keeping risk concentrated where it belongs: the scheduler, the persist-on-grade rule, and recovery after interruption.

**Claude (Product Strategist · Visionary) — Round 3**

Codex, I want to actually engage with what you said instead of just restating my round-2 position, because I think I owe you that after you called out that I hadn't been answered yet — and honestly, working through it, I think I owe you a real concession on one of these and a sharper version of my argument on the other.

On demo data: you're right that I was conflating two different things. There's "can we prove the day-boundary/DST math is correct" and "does a real user feel the payoff on first launch," and those don't actually need the same solution. The day-boundary/DST correctness claim is already fully discharged by the mandatory SM-2 unit test suite we both locked into DEC-next_steps_small-001 — that's a pure-module test with no SwiftData/SwiftUI dependency, and it's the actual proof, not a demo. And for the app-level integration check — does the shared due-function actually get used consistently by the UI, not reimplemented — I don't need seeded multi-day history for that at all. I can grade one card today, jump the simulator's system clock forward a day, relaunch, and confirm it shows up in the due list. That's a real, executable verification step, doesn't require shipping the demo-data feature, and it directly answers what I was actually worried about. So I'm updating: demo data comes out of this slice. Where I still want to hold a line is that it's fast-follow, not "maybe someday" — the moment we're proving multi-day trend behavior for real users (which the eventual stats charts absolutely need), we need it, and I don't want the cut here to accidentally read as "demo data is optional," because DEC-prompt_contract-003 already spent real design effort getting the badging/deletion contract right. And I like your one-tap create-deck-add-card-review flow as the actual substitute — that's the honest way to make an empty first run feel like a designed path rather than a dead end, and it costs us nothing we weren't already building.

On all-decks, I don't think I'm wrong yet, but I think there's a synthesis that gets you everything you actually said you wanted. Your objection was "three extra state dimensions: scope selection, cross-deck queue ordering, and per-card deck attribution in summaries" — but only one of those is actually UI-facing risk. The query itself — "give me cards due today, filtered to this set of decks" — has to exist as one function regardless, because DEC-initial_discussion-004 already requires one shared due-computation path used everywhere, and DEC-initial_discussion-005 already requires per-card deck identity to survive into the session layer for any future mixed-deck summary. If I write that function as `dueCards(scope: Set<Deck>)` from day one and just always call it with a one-element set in this slice, I get the general, correct, single-source-of-truth version for free — no throwaway code, no future rewrite — while completely dodging the actual risk you named: no scope-selector UI, no cross-deck queue ordering logic exposed to a user, no mixed-deck attribution math in the summary screen. There's no "Review All Decks" button in this slice, no mixed-deck session ever runs, so none of your three risk dimensions actually get exercised by a user or a test. That's not me sneaking scope back in, that's just writing the query correctly instead of writing a version we know we'll delete. If you've got a concrete reason the query itself is meaningfully riskier to write generally versus single-deck-specifically, I want to hear it, because I don't see one — but if you're just worried about the UI surface, I think we've already agreed on that by cutting the "all decks" entry point.

So here's my actual final position for this round: single-deck review only exposed in the UI, general scope-aware query underneath (not visible, not user-facing, just correctly architected), demo data cut from this slice entirely with the SM-2 test suite as the correctness proof and a manual clock-jump as the integration-verification substitute, and your one-tap empty-state onboarding flow ships as the emotional-payoff answer instead of demo data. I think that closes out both open items without either of us caving on the thing we actually cared about — you get a genuinely minimal user-facing surface, I get the query built right the first time and a real first-run experience that doesn't feel hollow.

**Demo data:** Claude conceded outright. **All-decks:** Claude found the synthesis that gives both sides what they actually wanted. The due-query gets built scope-general (`dueCards(scope: Set<Deck>)`) from day one, because DEC-initial_discussion-004 and -005 already require exactly that shared, deck-identity-preserving query to exist eventually — building it narrow now would just mean rewriting it later. **Stats** stays where round 2 left it: two inline numbers, no screen.

CONSENSUS: YES

## Final Output

**MVP slice:** A pure, fully-tested SM-2 module; deck create/edit/archive and keyboard-fast card create/edit; a single-deck review workflow (reveal → grade Again/Hard/Good/Easy → immediate synchronous persist → honest session summary); today's due count and retention rate shown as plain inline text (no dedicated screen); designed empty states for zero decks and zero due cards, reachable via a one-tap create-deck→add-card→review path. Underneath the single-deck UI, the due-card query is built scope-general (`dueCards(scope: Set<Deck>)`) so a future all-decks entry point is additive, not a rewrite.

**Must-have interactions:** deck create/rename/archive; card add/edit with Tab/Return keyboard flow; launch review for a chosen deck; tap-to-reveal and four-button grade; grade persists to SwiftData immediately, before advancing; force-quit/relaunch preserves every already-graded card's new schedule while ungraded cards remain due; end-of-session summary (reviewed count, again-rate, elapsed time); designed empty-state actions for 0 decks / 0 due cards.

**Cut list (explicit, fast-follow not abandoned):** all-decks review UI entry point (query exists, UI doesn't yet), the demo-data toggle, a dedicated Stats screen/tab, CSV import/export, the 30-day forecast and daily-history charts, the daily local reminder, the entire StoreKit subscription/paywall.

**Validation criteria:** (1) SM-2 unit tests pass for first-review, lapse-reset, ease-factor floor (1.3), and calendar-day/DST boundary, in a pure module with no SwiftData/SwiftUI imports; (2) full flow works with no network / in airplane mode, no hangs; (3) grade at least one card, force-quit, relaunch — confirm its new schedule is persisted and ungraded cards are still due; (4) grade a card today, advance the simulator's system clock by a day, relaunch — confirm it now appears due, proving the UI actually consumes the shared due-computation path rather than a parallel one; (5) a full single-deck session runs end-to-end from due-filter to an accurate summary screen; (6) zero-decks and zero-due-cards states both show the designed empty state with a working one-tap path into deck/card creation, never a blank screen.
